--- title: "Applying Periodic Boundary Conditions" description: "How do_periodic_segmentation_rust detects PBC equivalence groups — what extra_padding does, and how to inspect boundary maxima" image: tutorial_images/pbc_groups_concept.png jupyter: python3 execute: freeze: true --- ## Overview Periodic boundary conditions (PBC) are what turn a one-unit-cell snapshot of a MOF into a *truly infinite* material. mofography's job is to recognize that several distinct maxima/regions you see *inside the unit cell* are in fact **one cavity** wrapping through the periodic boundary. The new merged `do_periodic_segmentation_rust()` does this in one call. The PBC information is exposed through these output keys: | Key | What it is | |-----|------------| | `seg['pbc_groups']` | **list of sets** — `pbc_groups[i]` is the set of region labels wrapped into cavity `i` | | `seg['maxima_pbc']` | $(N, 3)$ array of **merged** maxima (one per group, not per fragment) | | `seg['regions_pbc']` | 3D label array of the **central cell** — regions already merged through PBC | | `seg['close_or_inside_maxima']` | $(N, 3)$ array — **voxel coords** of boundary maxima in the padded grid | | `seg['close_or_inside_regions']` | 1-based region labels of boundary-touching regions | This tutorial is the *PBC deep dive*. For the canonical 3-call workflow, see the [Quick Start tutorial](quick_cluster.qmd). ## Imports ::: {#20bf4a22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import mofography as mgr from ase.io import read import numpy as np ``` ::: ## Step 1: Load a MOF IRMOF-1 is the canonical PBC teaching example: the central pore sits at the cell center, and identical fragments appear at every face, edge, and corner — 8 fragments per cavity in total, *by Euler's formula for a cube*. ::: {#ba2e70fc .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} atoms = read("IRMOF-1.cif") print(f"Atoms: {len(atoms)}") print(f"Cell (Å): {atoms.cell.cellpar()[:3].round(2)}") print(f"Formula: {atoms.get_chemical_formula()}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Atoms: 424 Cell (Å): [25.83 25.83 25.83] Formula: C192H96O104Zn32 ``` ::: ::: ## Step 2: Compute the Distance Grid We use the thread-parallel Rust backend. `spacing=0.5 Å` is the sweet spot for most MOFs — fast and accurate enough for PBC detection. ::: {#e6293fa8 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} spacing = 0.5 # Å dgrid = mgr.dgrid_from_atoms_rust(atoms, spacing=spacing) print(f"Grid shape: {dgrid.shape} ({dgrid.size:,} voxels)") print(f"Void max: {dgrid.max():.1f} Å") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Grid shape: (52, 52, 52) (140,608 voxels) Void max: 7.5 Å ``` ::: ::: ## Step 3: One Call, Full PBC-Aware Segmentation `do_periodic_segmentation_rust` does maxima detection, watershed, PBC merging, and (optionally) window detection — all in one go. The merged maxima/regions are returned in the same dict. ::: {#3b56b5f6 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} dgrid_f32 = dgrid.astype(np.float32) seg = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust( dgrid_f32, atoms, mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5, spacing=spacing, compute_connections=True, # also build the pore graph extra_padding=5.0, # default — extra PBC halo (Å) watershed_backend="rust_det", disable_tqdm=True, ) ``` ::: ::: {#b117aa91 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("=== All output keys ===") for k in seg: v = seg[k] if hasattr(v, "shape"): print(f" {k:35s} ndarray shape={v.shape} dtype={v.dtype}") elif isinstance(v, dict): print(f" {k:35s} dict ({len(v)} entries)") elif isinstance(v, (list, tuple, set)): print(f" {k:35s} {type(v).__name__:6s} ({len(v)} items)") else: print(f" {k:35s} {type(v).__name__}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` === All output keys === dgrid ndarray shape=(52, 52, 52) dtype=float32 mat_atoms Atoms maxima_pbc ndarray shape=(8, 3) dtype=int64 regions_pbc ndarray shape=(52, 52, 52) dtype=uint32 maxima_info ndarray shape=(125, 7) dtype=int64 regions ndarray shape=(52, 52, 52) dtype=uint32 connections list (300 items) pbc_groups list (8 items) close_or_inside_maxima ndarray shape=(27, 3) dtype=int64 close_or_inside_regions ndarray shape=(27,) dtype=int64 unique_regions ndarray shape=(27,) dtype=uint32 maxima_pbc_dict dict (8 entries) all_maxima ndarray shape=(125, 3) dtype=int64 maxima_relative_locations ndarray shape=(125,) dtype=2} → {len(region_set)} region(s): {sorted(region_set)}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of PBC groups: 8 group 0 → 4 region(s): [1, 9, 10, 11] group 1 → 2 region(s): [2, 12] group 2 → 4 region(s): [3, 13, 14, 15] group 3 → 1 region(s): [4] group 4 → 4 region(s): [5, 16, 17, 18] group 5 → 2 region(s): [6, 19] group 6 → 2 region(s): [7, 20] group 7 → 8 region(s): [8, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27] ``` ::: ::: For IRMOF-1 there are **8 groups** — one central cavity, plus identical fragments at every face (×6), edge (×12), and corner (×8). The group sizes follow Euler's cube formula: $$ \text{fragments per cavity} = 1 + 6\cdot\tfrac{1}{2} + 12\cdot\tfrac{1}{4} + 8\cdot\tfrac{1}{8} = 8 $$ ### 4b. `maxima_pbc` — group representatives `maxima_pbc` is an $(N_\text{groups}, 3)$ array of *one* representative maximum per group — usually the highest-valued maximum within that group (use `all_maxima` for the full set of unmerged fragments). Row `i` of `maxima_pbc` corresponds to `pbc_groups[i]`. ::: {#63cfc83f .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} maxima_pbc = seg['maxima_pbc'] print(f"Shape: {maxima_pbc.shape}") print(f"\nGroup sizes (from pbc_groups):") for grp_idx, region_set in enumerate(seg['pbc_groups']): n_frag = len(region_set) px, py, pz = maxima_pbc[grp_idx] print(f" group {grp_idx:>2}: {n_frag} fragment(s) representative at " f"({px:5.1f}, {py:5.1f}, {pz:5.1f})") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Shape: (8, 3) Group sizes (from pbc_groups): group 0: 4 fragment(s) representative at ( 0.0, 25.0, 50.0) group 1: 2 fragment(s) representative at ( 0.0, 26.0, 25.0) group 2: 4 fragment(s) representative at ( 0.0, 50.0, 26.0) group 3: 1 fragment(s) representative at ( 24.0, 26.0, 25.0) group 4: 4 fragment(s) representative at ( 25.0, 0.0, 1.0) group 5: 2 fragment(s) representative at ( 26.0, 26.0, 0.0) group 6: 2 fragment(s) representative at ( 26.0, 51.0, 25.0) group 7: 8 fragment(s) representative at ( 51.0, 51.0, 0.0) ``` ::: ::: ### 4c. `regions_pbc` — central cell with PBC-merged labels `regions_pbc` is a 3D label array the **same shape as `dgrid`**, but with labels renumbered so that fragments on opposite walls of the same cavity share a single label. ::: {#170cabc6 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(f"regions_pbc shape: {seg['regions_pbc'].shape}") print(f"unique labels (excl. 0 background): " f"{int(seg['regions_pbc'].max())}") # Each label corresponds to one row in maxima_pbc import collections counts = collections.Counter(seg['regions_pbc'].ravel()) counts.pop(0, None) print(f"voxel count per PBC label:") for lbl, n in sorted(counts.items()): print(f" label {lbl:>2}: {n:>6,} voxels " f"({100*n/seg['regions_pbc'].size:.2f}%)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regions_pbc shape: (52, 52, 52) unique labels (excl. 0 background): 8 voxel count per PBC label: label 1: 20,344 voxels (14.47%) label 2: 9,104 voxels (6.47%) label 3: 18,760 voxels (13.34%) label 4: 8,352 voxels (5.94%) label 5: 18,760 voxels (13.34%) label 6: 18,760 voxels (13.34%) label 7: 9,104 voxels (6.47%) label 8: 9,104 voxels (6.47%) ``` ::: ::: This is the array you want to use for pore-size-distribution calculations: one label = one *physical* cavity. ## Step 5: Visualize PBC Groups Each PBC group should appear in the same color in the isosurface plot. ::: {#4e13fbe7 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} import plotly.graph_objects as go import plotly.express as px import mofography as mgr # Map region label → group id (so all members of a group share a color) label_to_group = {} for grp_idx, region_set in enumerate(seg['pbc_groups']): for lbl in region_set: label_to_group[int(lbl)] = int(grp_idx) # Re-color regions_pbc by PBC group for visualization regions_pbc_colored = np.zeros_like(seg['regions_pbc']) for lbl, grp in label_to_group.items(): regions_pbc_colored[seg['regions_pbc'] == lbl] = grp + 1 cscale = px.colors.qualitative.Pastel iso = mgr.plot_surface_dgrid( dgrid, ase_atoms=atoms, isovalue=1.75, cscale=cscale, opacity=1, stylize=True, region_labels=regions_pbc_colored, ) cell = mgr.plot_cell(atoms) fig = go.Figure(data=[iso, cell]) fig.update_layout(mgr.dark_layout, title="IRMOF-1: each color = one PBC group") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: You should see **8 distinct colors**, each appearing in 1 (center), 6 (face), 12 (edge), or 8 (corner) places — exactly the topology of a single cavity wrapped through the unit cell. ## Step 6: The `extra_padding` Parameter PBC merging works by *padding* the grid with ghost copies of the void, then asking the watershed to flood across the wall. If the padding is too thin, the flood misses the back-side maxima entirely and no group is formed. The total padding thickness is: $$ \text{padding} = \underbrace{\text{ceil}\!\left(\frac{\text{extra\_padding}}{\text{spacing}}\right)}_{\text{extra halo}} + \underbrace{\text{standard padding from pore radius}}_{\text{baseline}} $$ `extra_padding` is the user-tunable knob on top of the standard +5 Å cushion. Default is **5 Å** — sufficient for most MOFs. ### Effect of increasing `extra_padding` ::: {#7f7b62a7 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} def n_groups(seg_dict): return len(seg_dict['pbc_groups']) results = {} for pad in (0.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0): s = mgr.do_periodic_segmentation_rust( dgrid_f32, atoms, mask_thickness=0.05, h=0.2, min_distance=1.5, threshold_abs=1.5, spacing=spacing, compute_connections=False, extra_padding=pad, disable_tqdm=True, ) results[pad] = n_groups(s) print(f" extra_padding={pad:5.1f} Å → {results[pad]} PBC group(s)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` extra_padding= 0.0 Å → 8 PBC group(s) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` extra_padding= 2.0 Å → 8 PBC group(s) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` extra_padding= 5.0 Å → 8 PBC group(s) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` extra_padding= 10.0 Å → 8 PBC group(s) ``` ::: ::: :::: {.callout-tip} **How to spot a too-small `extra_padding`.** If you find *more* PBC groups than you expect (e.g. IRMOF-1 returning > 8), the PBC flood is *not* reaching across the wall. Increase in 1–2 Å steps. The cost is mostly memory — runtime grows with the padded grid volume. Note: IRMOF-1 returns 8 groups even at `extra_padding=0` because the standard halo (computed from `dgrid.max()` + a +5 Å cushion) is already generous — this rule applies to materials with **large mesopores** that exceed the standard halo. :::: ### Trade-off The standard PBC halo is already computed from `dgrid.max()` and a +5 Å cushion, so the *baseline* padding is generous for most MOFs. `extra_padding` is the user-tunable knob on top of that. | `extra_padding` | PBC detection | Memory | When to use | |---|---|---|---| | `0` *(smallest)* | works for most MOFs (IRMOF-1 included) | low | tight unit cells, large datasets | | `2–3` | extra safety for medium pores | low | when default-0 misses on a tricky case | | `5` *(default)* | matches the standard +5 Å cushion everywhere | moderate | start here for unknowns | | `10+` | very large mesopores that span the wall | high | NU-1000, MOFs with very wide channels | ## Step 7: Boundary Maxima — `close_or_inside_maxima` Some maxima sit *on* the cell wall (e.g. the centers of the face-fragments in IRMOF-1). These are the maxima most likely to need PBC merging. `close_or_inside_maxima` returns their 3D **voxel coordinates in the padded grid** (i.e. coordinates that extend *past* the unit cell — entries can be negative or larger than the grid shape when the maximum is in a ghost copy). ::: {#790c519d .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} pad = seg['input_params']['padding_thickness'] boundary_coords = seg['close_or_inside_maxima'] # (N, 3) padded-grid coords print(f"Boundary maxima count: {len(boundary_coords)}") print(f"Boundary maxima (padded-grid coords, first 5 rows):") print(boundary_coords[:5]) print() print("Their (x, y, z) positions in the unit cell (Å):") for ix, iy, iz in boundary_coords[:8]: # padded coords → central-cell coords → Å x = (ix - pad) * spacing y = (iy - pad) * spacing z = (iz - pad) * spacing on_wall = sum(coord < 0.5 or coord > atoms.cell.cellpar()[ax] - 0.5 for ax, coord in enumerate((x, y, z))) print(f" ({ix:>3},{iy:>3},{iz:>3}) → ({x:5.1f}, {y:5.1f}, {z:5.1f}) Å on {on_wall} wall(s)") print(f" ... ({len(boundary_coords) - 8} more)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Boundary maxima count: 27 Boundary maxima (padded-grid coords, first 5 rows): [[ 0 25 -2] [52 25 -2] [ 0 25 50] [52 25 50] [ 0 26 25]] Their (x, y, z) positions in the unit cell (Å): ( 0, 25, -2) → (-18.0, -5.5, -19.0) Å on 3 wall(s) ( 52, 25, -2) → ( 8.0, -5.5, -19.0) Å on 2 wall(s) ( 0, 25, 50) → (-18.0, -5.5, 7.0) Å on 2 wall(s) ( 52, 25, 50) → ( 8.0, -5.5, 7.0) Å on 1 wall(s) ( 0, 26, 25) → (-18.0, -5.0, -5.5) Å on 3 wall(s) ( 52, 26, 25) → ( 8.0, -5.0, -5.5) Å on 2 wall(s) ( 0, -2, 26) → (-18.0, -19.0, -5.0) Å on 3 wall(s) ( 0, 50, 26) → (-18.0, 7.0, -5.0) Å on 2 wall(s) ... (19 more) ``` ::: ::: ### `close_or_inside_regions` A list of **unmerged** region labels — i.e. labels in `seg['regions']` (the 3D grid *before* PBC merging), not in `regions_pbc`. These are the regions that sit near a unit-cell wall and *might* be PBC-mirrors of something on the other side — useful when validating your own segmentation outside the merged pipeline. boundary_reg = seg['close_or_inside_regions'] print(f"Boundary region labels (unmerged, first 10): " f"{sorted(int(x) for x in boundary_reg)[:10]}") print(f"Total unmerged region labels: " f"{int(seg['regions'].max())}") print(f"Fraction on boundary: " f"{100*len(boundary_reg)/max(1, int(seg['regions'].max())):.1f}%") ## Step 8: Validate with the Quick Cluster If you want a sanity check, run the [Quick Start tutorial](quick_cluster.qmd) on the same CIF. `maxima_pbc` count should match `len(seg['pbc_groups'])`, and the plotly visualization should show the same 8 colors per cavity. ## Where PBC Gets Tricky | Situation | Symptom | Fix | |---|---|---| | Large mesopore that crosses a wall | missed PBC merge → too many groups | raise `extra_padding` | | Two distinct cavities on opposite walls look similar | spurious merge | raise `min_distance` | | `regions_pbc` shows checkerboard pattern | grid too coarse, `spacing` too large | lower `spacing` to 0.3 Å | | More `close_or_inside_regions` than expected | MOF has many open channels — *correct* behavior | inspect manually | ## Parameter Reference (PBC-related) | Parameter | Default | Effect on PBC | |---|---|---| | `extra_padding` | 5.0 Å | halo beyond standard +5 Å — controls how far across the wall the flood reaches | | `wall_thickness` | 0.05 Å | the layer of voxels near the wall considered "wall" rather than "pore" | | `compute_connections` | True | also fill `seg['connections']`; needed for `pore_graph` | ## Next Steps - [Quick Start tutorial](quick_cluster.qmd) — full pore-graph in 3 calls - [Distance Grid tutorial](distance_grid.qmd) — how the input grid is built - [Connections and Windows](connections_and_windows.qmd) — windows between PBC groups - [Pore Graph tutorial](pore_graph.md) — convert segments + connections into a NetworkX graph
